description: Somos a DATA BEAT, uma equipe movida pela curiosidade, criatividade e inovação. Unimos tecnologia e ciência para transformar dados da Terra em sons, tornando as histórias do nosso planeta mais acessíveis, interativas e envolventes. Juntos, queremos inspirar as pessoas a descobrir e ouvir o nosso planeta de uma maneira totalmente nova.
summary:
SULCO is an interactive Earth data sonification studio that lets people explore our planet through sound, visuals, and accessible data tables. Built for “The Earth Information Jukebox” challenge, it transforms NASA temperature anomalies, satellite fire detections, and NOAA ocean temperature data into audible patterns.

Users can listen to changes, explore specific periods, and inspect the values behind each sound. Inspired by the groove of a vinyl record, SULCO aims to make Earth science more engaging and approachable for students, educators, and curious listeners, with English and Brazilian Portuguese interfaces and customizable accessibility features.
details:
SULCO begins with a question: what if we could listen to changes on Earth?

Scientific datasets can be difficult to interpret without technical knowledge. SULCO adds an auditory way to explore them, connecting official NASA visualizations with numerical records, interactive charts, and documented sound mappings. Its name refers to the groove of a vinyl record in Portuguese.

Climate

The climate experience explores NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 monthly global temperature anomalies relative to the 1951–1980 baseline.

Each valid month becomes a sine-wave note, with warmer anomalies producing higher pitches. Users can select periods, follow the timeline, and explore spiral and line views.

The mapping is explicit:

Frequency = 440 × 2^(anomaly / 4) Hz

A temperature anomaly of 0 °C corresponds to 440 Hz. Missing observations are skipped rather than interpolated.

Wildfires

The wildfire experience uses NASA FIRMS VIIRS detections from Suomi NPP and NOAA-21. Daily mean fire radiative power controls pitch, while detection counts control the number of pulses.

A map and data views provide geographic and numerical context. The application checks data availability before querying recent observations, since published satellite data may lag behind the calendar date.

Satellite detections do not represent unique fires or burned-area boundaries. Fire radiative power is expressed in megawatts.

The Problem

NASA and its partners provide valuable Earth observation data, but accessing these records does not always make them easy to understand. Temperature anomalies, satellite fire detections, and ocean measurements often require familiarity with scientific terminology and charts. This can make it difficult for students, educators, and the public to explore the data and connect individual measurements with changes over time.

Visual presentations alone can also create barriers for people who need alternative ways to access information.

Our Solution

SULCO turns Earth observation data into an interactive listening experience. It maps scientific measurements to sound, allowing users to hear changes while following synchronized charts, maps, and accessible data tables.

In the climate experience, higher temperature anomalies produce higher notes. In the wildfire experience, fire radiative power controls pitch and detection counts control pulses. In the ocean experience, changes in sampled sea surface temperature become changes in pitch.

Users can select periods, control playback, and inspect the values behind each sound. This connects an engaging sensory experience with traceable scientific information.

By combining sound, visuals, and text with English and Brazilian Portuguese interfaces, SULCO offers multiple ways to explore the same data. It supports science communication and classroom exploration while keeping sources, sound mappings, and scientific limitations visible.

Oceans

The ocean experience uses NOAA CoastWatch sea surface temperature data delivered through ERDDAP. Users can explore selected regions and recent periods.

The application calculates daily summaries from sampled grid points and maps temperature to pitch. These summaries describe the queried samples rather than an area-weighted estimate of the entire ocean.

Implementation

Built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and the Web Audio API, SULCO generates audio directly in the browser.

Climate data is fetched from NASA, with an identified local backup when the remote source is unavailable. FIRMS credentials remain on the server.

Users can explore data through interactive charts, playback controls, maps, and numerical views. The climate Data Explorer allows users to inspect values and download the selected data as CSV.

Accessibility

Accessibility features include keyboard navigation, text equivalents for sound events, accessible data tables, adjustable contrast and text size, reduced motion, and playback controls.

Audio starts only after user interaction. The interface supports English and Brazilian Portuguese, allowing users to choose their preferred language.

SULCO combines sound, visuals, and text to provide multiple ways to explore the same scientific information.

Purpose and Scientific Limitations

SULCO is designed for science communication and exploratory learning. It aims to help students, educators, and the public engage with Earth observations through an interactive experience.

Its sound mappings are artistic choices documented alongside the data. They are not physical laws or predictive models.

The application explains limitations so listeners can connect what they hear to what the measurements actually represent. Global temperature averages conceal regional differences, satellite fire detections do not count unique fires, and sampled ocean summaries do not represent the entire ocean.
